summary: Describes the assumptions, problem statement, and goals for carrying IP over IEEE 802.15.4 networks, which are low-power and small. It lists an initial set of goals, not a final one. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Tiny battery-powered gadgets want to join the Internet too. This note lists the problems that come with putting such small things online.

questions: why is ipv6 hard on ieee 802.15.4
subtitle: Why putting IPv6 on tiny, battery-powered 802.15.4 radios is hard, and what has to be solved first.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.15.4 devices are small, cheap, battery-powered and send tiny frames, which does not fit the way IPv6 normally works.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes what LoWPANs look like, lists the problems with running IP over them, and sets out a prioritized list of eight goals, starting with fragmentation and header compression.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational problem statement, not a protocol. The goals are described as an initial set only, and some are work for other bodies than the IETF.

today: RFC 4919 is an Informational RFC from August 2007. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
A low-power wireless personal area network (LoWPAN) is made of devices that follow the IEEE 802.15.4-2003 standard. Such devices have short range, low bit rate, low power and low cost, and many are limited in computing power, memory or energy.

The RFC gives an overview of LoWPANs, explains how they benefit from IP and in particular IPv6, states the assumptions, describes the problems, and defines goals in priority order. It admits that not every goal is a suitable task for the IETF; they are written down to give the larger picture and to help coordinate with outside organizations.
sections.eli5: Some gadgets are very small and run on batteries. This note explains why they need the Internet and lists the trouble that comes with that.

sections.title: What a LoWPAN Looks Like
sections.content:
The RFC lists ten characteristics. The most important for design are the frame size and the data rate. The maximum physical layer packet is 127 bytes, which leaves a maximum MAC frame of 102 octets. Link-layer security takes up to 21 octets in the AES-CCM-128 case (9 and 13 for AES-CCM-32 and AES-CCM-64), leaving 81 octets for data.

Other traits are support for 16-bit short or 64-bit extended MAC addresses, star and mesh topologies, battery operation, low cost, a very large number of devices, ad-hoc placement, unreliable devices and long sleep periods during which a device cannot communicate.

The three physical layers run at 250 kbps (2.4 GHz), 40 kbps (915 MHz) and 20 kbps (868 MHz).
sections.eli5: The messages these gadgets send are like very short postcards, they talk slowly, and they nap a lot to save battery.

sections.title: Assumptions and the Case for IP
sections.content:
The RFC assumes applications mostly send small amounts of data, although the protocols do not forbid bulk transfers. It expects two kinds of devices: extremely limited Reduced Function Devices (RFDs) and a smaller number of more capable Full Function Devices (FFDs), which may be mains powered and help RFDs with coordination, forwarding and links to other networks.

Five benefits of IP are assumed: existing infrastructure can be used, IP technology is proven, its specifications are open, diagnostic and management tools already exist, and IP devices connect to other IP networks without translation gateways or proxies.
sections.eli5: Big helper devices look after the tiny ones. Using the same language as the rest of the Internet means no translator is needed in the middle.

sections.title: Problems With IP on LoWPANs
sections.content:
Six problem areas are described. IP connectivity: IPv6 offers autoconfiguration, a large address space and an address format that can subsume IEEE 802.15.4 addresses, but headers must be compressed because packets are so small. Topologies: mesh and star must both work, and a mesh routing protocol must add little or no overhead to data packets, keep chatter low and need little memory.

Limited packet size: control packets should fit in one 802.15.4 frame, and IPv6's requirement to reassemble packets of 1280 octets may be hard for devices with little RAM. Configuration and management should be minimal and self-healing. Service discovery needs simple protocols, possibly new ones. Security: 802.15.4 mandates AES link-layer security but leaves out bootstrapping, key management and higher-layer security.
sections.eli5: If every postcard is tiny, the address label can eat most of the space. Gadgets also cannot be set up by hand one by one, so they must mostly set themselves up.

sections.title: The Eight Goals
sections.content:
The goals are listed in priority order, with a common aim of reducing packet overhead, bandwidth, processing and power use.

  1. Fragmentation and reassembly layer: frames carry as little as 81 bytes, far below the IPv6 minimum of 1280 octets, so an adaptation layer below IP is needed.
  2. Header compression: with a 40-octet IPv6 header, only 41 octets remain, leaving 33 for data over UDP (8-octet header) and 21 over TCP (20-octet header).
  3. Address autoconfiguration: stateless autoconfiguration is attractive, and a method to build an interface identifier from the device's EUI-64 is needed.
  4. Mesh routing protocol: existing ad-hoc protocols use large addresses; AODV needs 48 octets for a route request over IPv6.
  5. Network management: SNMP could be reused, but SNMPv3 needs further study.
  6. Implementation considerations should be documented.
  7. Application and higher-layer considerations: heavy XML-based protocols such as SOAP may not suit LoWPANs.
  8. Security considerations: threats should be documented, and bootstrapping considered.
sections.eli5: The to-do list starts with the biggest problem: squeezing big Internet messages into tiny frames, by cutting them up and shrinking the labels.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
6LoWPAN applications often need confidentiality and integrity protection, which can sit at the application, transport, network or link layer. Code size, power, complexity and bandwidth all constrain the choice. The RFC says a threat model must be developed first, naming man-in-the-middle and denial of service attacks as examples.

Initial key establishment (bootstrapping) is treated as outside 6LoWPAN, but later key management and securing data traffic are in scope, and options such as TLS and IKE/IPsec must be weighed against the constraints. Link-layer AES is attractive because most 802.15.4 devices already support it. Older modes (ECB, CBC, OFB, CFB) give only confidentiality, so the RFC prefers modes such as CCM* that also protect integrity.

For network-layer security it contrasts end-to-end IPsec transport mode with IPsec tunnel mode through a gateway, noting that the latter's larger headers matter at 6LoWPAN frame sizes.
sections.eli5: Secret locks help, but they must be light enough for a tiny gadget to carry. Some locks hide the message and also show if someone changed it, and those are best.
